passages.happening:
Early in the morning Jesus is teaching in the temple courts, and the people have gathered around him (verses 1-2). The scribes and Pharisees bring in a woman and make her stand in front of everyone. “Teacher, this woman was caught in the act of adultery,” they say. “In the Law Moses commanded us to stone such a woman. So what do You say?” (verses 4-5). John tells us why they ask: “They said this to test Him, in order to have a basis for accusing Him” (verse 6).

Jesus does not answer at once. He bends down and writes on the ground with his finger. They keep pressing him. So he stands up and says, “Let him who is without sin among you be the first to cast a stone at her” (verse 7). Then he bends down and writes again.

One by one they leave, “beginning with the older ones” (verse 9). At last only Jesus is left, with the woman still standing there. He asks her, “Woman, where are your accusers? Has no one condemned you?” She answers, “No one, Lord.” Then Jesus says, “Then neither do I condemn you,” and, “Now go and sin no more” (verses 10-11).
passages.hearers:
Where is the man? The Law of Moses said that in adultery both the man and the woman must die. The accusers say she was caught ‘in the act’, so the man was there too. Yet they bring only her. That alone shows this was not a careful search for justice. The woman is being used. She is made to stand in front of a crowd while men argue over her life, and the man who shared her sin is nowhere in the story.

The question was a trap with two sides. If Jesus said ‘Stone her’, he would seem harsh, and he would be calling for a death sentence that, under Roman rule, the leaders could not lawfully carry out. Later in John they say to Pilate, “We are not permitted to execute anyone” (18:31). If he said ‘Let her go’, they could say he set aside the Law of Moses. Either answer would give them a charge against him.

The Law also had rules for a death sentence. There had to be two or three witnesses, and the witnesses had to throw the first stones. Jesus' answer takes up that very rule and turns it. Let the first stone come from someone without sin.

What did Jesus write on the ground? No one knows. John does not say. Some have suggested he wrote the accusers' sins. An old suggestion links it to Jeremiah, who says that those who turn away from the LORD ‘will be written in the dust’. Others think he was simply refusing to answer on their terms. Any of these may be right, and none can be proved.

Why do the older ones leave first? John does not explain that either. Perhaps the longer a person has lived, the harder it is to claim to be without sin.

‘Woman’ was not a rude word. Jesus uses it for his own mother (2:4). It is a respectful way to speak to her, perhaps the first respect she has been shown that morning.
passages.ot: The Law said, “both the adulterer and the adulteress must surely be put to death” (Leviticus 20:10), and again, “both the man who slept with her and the woman must die” (Deuteronomy 22:22). It also guarded against a quick death sentence: “On the testimony of two or three witnesses a man shall be put to death, but he shall not be executed on the testimony of a lone witness” (Deuteronomy 17:6), and “The hands of the witnesses shall be the first in putting him to death” (Deuteronomy 17:7). Jeremiah wrote, “All who turn away will be written in the dust” (Jeremiah 17:13). And the commandment stands behind the whole scene: “You shall not commit adultery” (Exodus 20:14).
passages.hard:
Is this story part of John? Many Bibles print it in brackets or with a note, and readers deserve a plain answer. The oldest copies of John do not have it. The early papyri P66 and P75, from around AD 200, and the great fourth-century books known as Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus go straight from 7:52 to 8:12. The first Greek copy known to include it is Codex Bezae, from the fifth century. Later copies place it in different spots: after John 7:36, at the very end of John, or after Luke 21:38. Jerome kept it in his Latin translation, and he said it was found in many Greek and Latin copies. So the story was kept, above all in the Latin tradition. The Berean Standard Bible prints it and marks it as a later addition.

The story itself was known early. Eusebius, the church historian of the early 300s, reports that Papias, a bishop of the early second century, told a story of a woman accused of many sins before the Lord. Many think this is the same story, though Papias's version may have differed in its details.

How do Christians regard it? The common view, held by most scholars across the churches, is that it is an ancient and true story of Jesus that was not originally in this place. The church remembered it, and it was later written into John. A small number of scholars hold that it was part of John from the start and was dropped from some copies. Others think it may be taught as a true account of Jesus but should not be preached as Scripture in the full sense. The Roman Catholic Church accepts it as Scripture. These notes take no side.

None of this is cause for alarm. Nothing in the Christian faith rests on this passage alone. What it shows of Jesus, mercy that comes first and a call to a new life that follows, is found all through the Gospels. And the church has always said openly where its copies differ.
passages.asks:
Notice what Jesus does not do. He does not make the woman into a lesson for the crowd. He waits until the crowd is gone, and only then does he speak to her, and he speaks to her as a person. Nothing in this story gives anyone leave to shame anyone.

Jesus holds two things together. His first word is “Then neither do I condemn you.” His second is “Now go and sin no more.” He does not wave her sin away, and he does not crush her with it. The mercy comes first, and the call that follows does not cancel it.

If you carry shame about something sexual, this story is for you. The one person in the scene who was without sin did not pick up a stone. If what happened to you was not your choice, it is not your sin, and you deserve safety and help from someone you trust. And if you have ever been one of the people holding a stone, the story asks you to put it down and walk away quietly, as the older men did.

passages.t: I am the light of the world
passages.happening:
Jesus speaks to the people again: “I am the light of the world. Whoever follows Me will never walk in the darkness, but will have the light of life” (verse 12).

The Pharisees object: “You are testifying about Yourself; Your testimony is not valid” (verse 13). Jesus answers that his witness is true, because he knows where he came from and where he is going, and they do not (verse 14). He is not a lone witness. “I am One who testifies about Myself, and the Father, who sent Me, also testifies about Me” (verse 18).

“Where is Your Father?” they ask. He answers, “You do not know Me or My Father.” And he adds, “If you knew Me, you would know My Father as well” (verse 19). John adds that he said this while teaching near the treasury, and still “no one seized Him, because His hour had not yet come” (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
In the oldest copies of John, this verse comes straight after 7:52, where the leaders sneered that no prophet comes out of Galilee. Read that way, Jesus' answer is striking. They doubt he is even a prophet. He says he is the light of the whole world.

The setting matters too. The Feast of Tabernacles was ending or had just ended (7:2, 7:37). The Mishnah, a collection of Jewish teaching written down around AD 200, describes great lamps lit in the Court of the Women during the feast. How much of that was done in Jesus' day is not certain. The treasury, where the offering chests stood, was probably in the same court. If so, Jesus called himself the light of the world close to the place where those lamps had burned.

The feast also remembered the wilderness, when Israel followed a pillar of fire by night. ‘Whoever follows Me’ would remind hearers of that. Light was not only for looking at. It was for following.

The argument about witnesses comes from the Law. One witness was not enough to settle a matter. Jesus answers on their own terms. There are two witnesses here: himself and the Father.

‘His hour had not yet come’ is a thread that runs through John (2:4, 7:30). His enemies are not in control of what happens to him. The hour will come, at the cross, and it will come when the Father wills it.
passages.ot: On the way out of Egypt, “the LORD went before them in a pillar of cloud to guide their way by day, and in a pillar of fire to give them light by night” (Exodus 13:21). The Psalms sing, “The LORD is my light and my salvation” (Psalm 27:1). Isaiah promised a servant whom God would make “a light for the nations, to bring My salvation to the ends of the earth” (Isaiah 49:6), and wrote, “The people walking in darkness have seen a great light” (Isaiah 9:2). The rule about witnesses is in Deuteronomy: “A matter must be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses” (Deuteronomy 19:15).
passages.hard: Does Jesus contradict himself? In 5:31 he said, “If I testify about Myself, My testimony is not valid.” Here he says, “Even if I testify about Myself, My testimony is valid” (verse 14). In chapter 5 he was granting the rule for the sake of argument: a man's word about himself is not enough on its own, so he called other witnesses, John the Baptist, his works, the Father and the Scriptures. Here he goes further. His word is true because he knows where he came from. And in both places he says the same thing in the end. He never stands alone. The Father stands with him.
passages.asks: Light is not only something to admire. It is something to walk by. Jesus does not promise his followers that they will understand everything. He promises that they will not walk in the darkness. If the way ahead looks dark to you, the question this passage asks is not how much you can see, but whom you are following.

passages.t: Unless you believe that I am He
passages.happening:
Jesus says, “I am going away, and you will look for Me, but you will die in your sin. Where I am going, you cannot come” (verse 21). His hearers wonder aloud, “Will He kill Himself?” (verse 22).

He answers, “You are from below; I am from above. You are of this world; I am not of this world” (verse 23). Then he warns them: “For unless you believe that I am He, you will die in your sins” (verse 24).

“Who are You?” they ask. “Just what I have been telling you from the beginning,” he replies (verse 25). They do not understand that he is speaking of the Father (verse 27). So he tells them, “When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am He, and that I do nothing on My own, but speak exactly what the Father has taught Me” (verse 28). The Father has not left him alone, because he always does what pleases him (verse 29). John ends this part simply: “As Jesus spoke these things, many believed in Him” (verse 30).
passages.hearers:
‘The Jews’ in verse 22 are the same people Jesus has been arguing with, called the Pharisees in verse 13. In John the phrase often means the particular people in the scene, not the whole people. John's book page explains this.

Their question about suicide shows how far apart they are. He speaks of going back to the Father. They can only imagine a man going where they cannot follow by taking his own life. John often lets a misunderstanding show the gap between Jesus' words and his hearers' ears.

‘I am He’ is two words in Greek, egō eimi, ‘I am’. The Berean Standard Bible adds ‘He’ to make the English read smoothly. In ordinary speech the words could simply mean ‘I am the one’. The blind man uses them that way in the next chapter (9:9). But a hearer who knew the Scriptures in Greek would also hear an echo. In the Greek Old Testament God says ‘I am’ of himself, as when he says, through Isaiah, that his people should know ‘that I am He’. Jesus may mean both at once, and the end of this chapter makes the second meaning plain.

‘Lifted up’ is one of John's words with two sides. It means being raised on a cross, and it also means being exalted, lifted high in honor. Jesus used it in 3:14, and he will use it again in 12:32-33. In John the cross is not only the place of his death. It is where people will see who he is.
passages.ot: In Isaiah God tells his people he has chosen them “so that you may consider and believe Me and understand that I am He” (Isaiah 43:10). In Deuteronomy he says, “See now that I am He; there is no God besides Me” (Deuteronomy 32:39). And Isaiah 41:4 ends with the same words, “I am He.” ‘Lifted up’ recalls the snake in the wilderness: “Moses made a bronze snake and mounted it on a pole” (Numbers 21:9), the picture Jesus used in John 3:14.
passages.hard: ‘You will die in your sins’ sounds severe. To whom is it said? To people who were standing in front of Jesus, hearing him, and refusing him. It is a warning, not a gloating. John's point is that sin is not only wrong things done. It is also a turning away from the one who came to save (3:17). The warning comes with an open door: ‘unless you believe’. And this very passage ends with many believing.
passages.asks: Jesus says, “He has not left Me alone” (verse 29). Even facing hostile questions, he was not alone. If you feel alone in a hard place, his words are worth holding: the Father did not leave the Son, and those who belong to the Son are not left either.

passages.t: The truth will set you free
passages.happening:
Now Jesus speaks to “the Jews who had believed Him” (verse 31). He says, “If you continue in My word, you are truly My disciples. Then you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free” (verses 31-32).

They answer, “We are Abraham’s descendants.” And they add, “We have never been slaves to anyone. How can You say we will be set free?” (verse 33).

Jesus replies, “Truly, truly, I tell you, everyone who sins is a slave to sin” (verse 34). A slave is not a permanent member of the family, but a son belongs to it forever (verse 35). “So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed” (verse 36). Then the tone changes. He tells them, “I know you are Abraham’s descendants, but you are trying to kill Me because My word has no place within you” (verse 37).
passages.hearers:
Notice who is spoken to. Not unbelievers, and not the Jewish people as a whole, but people who had just believed. Jesus is testing what kind of faith it is. Will they stay with his word when it costs them something? The harsh words that follow in this chapter are spoken to these particular hearers, in this particular argument.

‘We have never been slaves to anyone’ is a surprising thing to say. Israel remembered every Passover that their people had been slaves in Egypt, and in Jesus' day they lived under Roman rule. They probably meant that no one owned them inside. They belonged to God alone, as children of Abraham. Jesus says there is a deeper slavery that birth cannot break: slavery to sin.

The picture of the household was easy to follow. A slave lived in the house but could be sold. A son belonged to the family for good. Jesus is the Son of the house, and he can give others a son's freedom.

‘The truth will set you free’ is one of the most quoted lines in the Bible. It is carved, for example, in the entrance hall of the CIA's original headquarters building. But it is often quoted without its first half. In John the promise belongs to those who ‘continue in My word’. The truth here is not just facts. Jesus will say, “I am the way and the truth and the life” (14:6). The truth that frees is found in knowing him.
passages.ot: God introduced himself at Sinai as the one who freed slaves: “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery” (Exodus 20:2). The Law built on it: “Because the Israelites are My servants, whom I brought out of the land of Egypt, they are not to be sold as slaves” (Leviticus 25:42). God promised Abraham, “all the families of the earth will be blessed through you” (Genesis 12:3). Jesus is speaking of a new exodus, from a deeper slavery.
passages.hard: Does this mean Jesus' followers never struggle with sin? No. Paul wrote to Christians that “you once were slaves to sin.” Then he wrote, “You have been set free from sin and have become slaves to righteousness” (Romans 6:17-18), and then spent chapters helping them live it out. Freedom is given at once, and it is learned over a lifetime. The point of verse 34 is not that any one sin makes a person hopeless. It is that no one can free himself. Only the Son can.
passages.asks: Where are you bound in ways you would rather not admit? Jesus' hearers insisted they had never been slaves. Freedom begins with honesty about the chains. And it continues by staying with his word, day after day, long after the first moment of belief.

passages.happening:
“Abraham is our father,” they reply. “If you were children of Abraham,” Jesus answers, “you would do the works of Abraham. But now you are trying to kill Me, a man who has told you the truth that I heard from God. Abraham never did such a thing” (verses 39-40).

“We are not illegitimate children,” they declare. “Our only Father is God Himself” (verse 41). Jesus says, “If God were your Father, you would love Me, for I have come here from God” (verse 42). Then come the hardest words in the chapter: “You belong to your father, the devil, and you want to carry out his desires. He was a murderer from the beginning, refusing to uphold the truth, because there is no truth in him” (verse 44).

Jesus asks, “Which of you can prove Me guilty of sin? If I speak the truth, why do you not believe Me?” (verse 46). And he ends: “Whoever belongs to God hears the words of God” (verse 47).
passages.hearers:
In the ancient world a son was expected to be like his father and to do what his father did. Jesus has already said this of himself: “whatever the Father does, the Son also does” (5:19). So the argument here is not about birth. Jesus grants that his hearers are Abraham's descendants (verse 37). The question is whose likeness they show. Abraham welcomed God's messengers and trusted God's word. These hearers, Jesus says, are trying to kill the messenger.

‘A murderer from the beginning’ and ‘the father of lies’ point back to the first pages of the Bible. In the garden the serpent told the first lie: “You will not surely die” (Genesis 3:4). Death came into the world through that lie. Some readers also think of Cain, who killed his brother. To seek to kill someone because he tells you the truth, Jesus says, is to take after the liar and the murderer, whoever your ancestors are.

This was a heated argument inside one people. Jesus is Jewish, his disciples are Jewish, and so are the people he argues with. Insults fly both ways. In the next verses his opponents call him a Samaritan with a demon (verse 48).
passages.ot: Abraham's faith was the mark of his family: “Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness” (Genesis 15:6). The prophets spoke hard words to their own people when they turned from God. Isaiah cried, “Alas, O sinful nation, a people laden with iniquity, a brood of evildoers, children of depravity!” (Isaiah 1:4). The words of verse 44 stand in that line: a warning spoken from inside Israel to people inside Israel. And behind ‘the father of lies’ stands the serpent's lie in Genesis 3.
passages.hard:
This verse has been used terribly. For centuries it was used to call Jewish people children of the devil, and to justify hatred, expulsions and murder. In the 1930s Nazi propaganda put it in a book for German children. That reading is false, and Christians must reject it plainly. This site rejects it. Never a word against the Jewish people.

Read where it stands, the verse says something else. Jesus is speaking to particular people, ‘the Jews who had believed Him’ (verse 31), who are now, he says, trying to kill him (verses 37 and 40). The charge is about what they are doing, not about who their parents were. Jesus himself is a Jew, and so are his disciples and the man who wrote this book. In this same Gospel Jesus says, “salvation is from the Jews” (4:22).

The language is the hard language of a quarrel inside one people, in the manner of the prophets. Other Jewish writings of the time spoke the same way. The Community Rule, one of the Dead Sea Scrolls, told its members to hate ‘the sons of darkness’ and cursed ‘the men of the lot of Belial’, names that took in everyone outside their own community, fellow Jews included. Scholars who study ancient argument note that rival groups commonly called one another liars and worse. That does not make the words gentle. It shows they were said by insiders to insiders.

And the New Testament uses the same language of Christians. Jesus calls Peter ‘Satan’ (Mark 8:33), and he says of one of the Twelve, “one of you is a devil” (6:70). The first letter of John says it of anyone who makes a practice of sin: “The one who practices sin is of the devil,” and “By this the children of God are distinguished from the children of the devil” (1 John 3:8, 10). In 1965 the Catholic Church's Second Vatican Council said that ‘the Jews should not be presented as rejected or accursed by God, as if this followed from the Holy Scriptures’. Most churches teach the same. The verse is a warning to every reader, Christians first of all, about what happens when religious people refuse the truth and set out to destroy the one who speaks it.
passages.asks: The question in this passage is not whose blood runs in us. It is whose likeness we show. Being born into a faithful family does not make anyone faithful, and going to church does not either. Jesus asks what we do when the truth is spoken to us, especially when it is spoken against us. Do we listen, or do we look for a way to silence the speaker?

passages.t: Before Abraham was born, I am
passages.happening:
His opponents answer with insults: “Are we not right to say that You are a Samaritan and You have a demon?” (verse 48). “I do not have a demon,” Jesus replies, “but I honor My Father, and you dishonor Me” (verse 49). Then he makes a promise: “Truly, truly, I tell you, if anyone keeps My word, he will never see death” (verse 51).

They are sure now that he is mad. Abraham died, and so did the prophets. “Are You greater than our father Abraham?” they ask. “Who do You claim to be?” (verse 53).

Jesus says, “Your father Abraham rejoiced that he would see My day. He saw it and was glad” (verse 56). They scoff: “You are not yet fifty years old, and You have seen Abraham?” (verse 57). And then: “Truly, truly, I tell you,” Jesus declares, “before Abraham was born, I am!” (verse 58). At this they pick up stones to throw at him. But he is hidden and goes out of the temple area (verse 59).
passages.hearers:
To call a Jew a Samaritan was an insult. Samaritans were seen as outsiders who had turned from Jerusalem's temple (4:9, 4:20). To say he had a demon was to call him mad. The crowd had already said it once (7:20).

‘Never see death’ does not mean his followers will not die. Jesus is speaking of the death that ends a person's life with God. In chapter 11 he will say it plainly at a graveside.

How did Abraham ‘see’ Jesus' day? John does not say. On the mountain Abraham told Isaac, “God Himself will provide the lamb” (Genesis 22:8). Some later Jewish writings also say that God showed Abraham the future. One of them, known as 4 Ezra and written near the end of the first century, says that God loved Abraham and showed him the end of the times secretly by night. Jesus says the day Abraham longed for was his.

‘Not yet fifty’ is a round number. It means, ‘You are not even an old man.’

Then the words that stopped the argument. ‘Before Abraham was born’ uses a Greek verb that means ‘came to be’. Abraham came to be at a point in time. But Jesus does not say ‘I was’. He says ‘I am’. His hearers understood it as a claim no man could make. That is why they picked up stones. The Law ordered stoning for anyone who blasphemed the name of the LORD.
passages.ot: At the burning bush God said to Moses, “I AM WHO I AM. This is what you are to say to the Israelites: ‘I AM has sent me to you.’” (Exodus 3:14). The Psalms speak of God's life without beginning: “Before the mountains were born or You brought forth the earth and the world, from everlasting to everlasting You are God” (Psalm 90:2). Isaiah has God say ‘I am He’ again and again (Isaiah 43:10). And the Law said, “Whoever blasphemes the name of the LORD must surely be put to death; the whole assembly must surely stone him” (Leviticus 24:16).
passages.hard:
What is Jesus claiming in verse 58? Most Christians, and most translations, read it as a claim to have no beginning: Abraham came to be, but Jesus simply is. Many hear in it the name God gave Moses at the bush, ‘I AM’. Others think the echo is mainly Isaiah's ‘I am He’, where God declares that he alone is God. Scholars debate which echo is stronger. Either way the claim is the same in kind. It is something only God can say of himself, and the stones show that the hearers understood it that way.

The church came to confess what these hearers refused. When teachers in the fourth century said the Son had a beginning, the church answered with the Nicene Creed. In the older English wording printed on this site it confesses him as ‘very God of very God, begotten, not made, being of one substance with the Father’. This is what the creeds bind all Christians to confess.
passages.asks: ‘Who do You claim to be?’ is the question of this whole chapter, and of the whole Gospel. The hearers saw only a man not yet fifty. Jesus said he was before Abraham. There is no middle way left by these words. Either he was terribly wrong, or he is who he said. The chapter asks each reader to answer the question for themselves, honestly, and not to settle it by picking up stones.
